props.title: Land of the Dead
props.initialSlug: Zombies siege humanity's last fortified city

sections.content: George Romero's Land of the Dead marks a fascinating evolution in zombie cinema, building on his groundbreaking Night of the Living Dead (1968). This fourth entry in Romero's Dead series tackles class warfare head-on, depicting a feudal society where wealthy elites live in a luxury high-rise while poor survivors struggle in the slums. The film's intelligent zombies, led by "Big Daddy," represent an oppressed underclass rising up against exploitation - a sharp critique of post-9/11 American society that builds on themes Romero explored in Dawn of the Dead (1978).

sections.content: The film's setting of "Fiddler's Green" - a luxury tower controlled by Dennis Hopper's ruthless capitalist Kaufman - draws clear parallels to real-world wealth inequality. This class consciousness aligns with other post-apocalyptic films like Snowpiercer (2013) and High-Rise (2015), but Romero's zombie lens makes the social commentary particularly biting. The evolving intelligence of the undead, building on hints from Day of the Dead (1985), suggests humanity's real monsters are those hoarding resources and power.

Technically, Land of the Dead represents Romero's biggest budget and most polished production. The practical zombie effects by KNB continue the tradition of The Walking Dead (2010-2022) and earlier Romero films, while the night raids and fortress city echo elements of 28 Days Later (2002). Yet Romero maintains his signature social consciousness, making this both a worthy Dead entry and a bridge to modern zombie cinema. SUBHEAD: Evolution of the Modern Zombie

sections.content: Land of the Dead arrived as zombie films were evolving beyond Romero's original template. While films like [REC] (2007) and Zombieland (2009) would take the genre in new directions, Romero's final Dead film maintained his focus on social commentary through horror. The film's depiction of zombies gaining intelligence influenced later works like Warm Bodies (2013) and The Girl with All the Gifts (2016), showing how the genre could explore humanity through its monsters.
